answers.answer: Fifty boxes of earth (the invoice reads 'Fifty cases of common earth'), shipped to Whitby and then taken to Carfax, near Purfleet. Twenty-one were later removed from Carfax: six to 197 Chicksand Street, Mile End New Town; six to Jamaica Lane, Bermondsey; and nine from a house in Piccadilly (five on the first load, four on the second, as the carter Bloxam told Harker). Twenty-nine were left at Carfax.

First mentioned on 26 July 1893 by Mina, in her journal: Lucy 'has lately taken to her old habit of walking in her sleep', so the habit predates the store. Mina also records Mrs. Westenra's worry about it and the decision to lock the door. The store has no earlier mention.

Only one: Lucy's diary entry of 12 September 1893 (e0106). Her other letters and diary entries (9 May, 24 May, 19 Aug, 23 Aug, 25 Aug, 9 Sep, 17 Sep, and the memorandum of 17 Sep) name Arthur, and I checked the variants Arthur, Art, Holmwood and Godalming.

Four transfusions, in order: (1) Arthur Holmwood, 7 September, with Van Helsing performing and Seward assisting; (2) Dr. John Seward, 10 September; (3) Van Helsing, 13 September ('I shall provide'); (4) Quincey Morris, 18 September, after Arthur's telegram brought him to Hillingham.

The garlic came from Haarlem, from Van Helsing's friend Vanderpool's glass-houses, where herbs grow all year. Van Helsing ordered it by telegram and arranged it, placing the flowers in Lucy's window and making her wreath, with Seward helping him deck the room. Lucy's later diary says a boxful came from Haarlem every day.

First in the store on 5 May 1893, in Jonathan Harker's journal at the Castle, where he lists Slovak and Serbian words he heard in Bistritz: 'vrolok' and 'vlkoslak' 'for something that is either were-wolf or vampire'. The English 'vampire' there is Harker's own gloss, not a local word.

One document only: a letter dated 25 May 1893 from Quincey P. Morris to Arthur Holmwood, signed 'QUINCEY P. MORRIS', inviting Arthur to a camp-fire with Seward and recalling their old adventures. The only other item under his name is the telegram from Holmwood to him, so the store holds nothing else in his own hand.

experience: The tool's warnings were the most useful part. For the earth-box and transfusion questions, DECOMPOSITION_REQUIRED and the CONTINUES warnings sent me to read around passages, and the grep counts (38 passages in 22 entries for the boxes) showed where the material was. The single-source and OFF_QUESTION warnings kept me from citing the top search hit for the earth question, since e0180.18 (the Piccadilly visit) and e0022.4 (the box with the Count) were on-topic but not the answer. The date-ordered output of grep made the first sleepwalking and vampire mentions easy to find. What got in the way: `list --with` without `--by-entry` returned single passages, and I first read that as an entry count, so I had to repeat the query. The name-variant advice for negation was right, since 'Art' is a word-start match that also catches Arthur. A `read` of an ID I had guessed (e0107.5) crashed with a KeyError and printed a traceback showing the tool's source path; I did not open it. search returned unrelated passages for the garlic and Quincey questions, so grep was more reliable for enumerating. I wished the tool said which entries were a telegram's sender versus recipient, and that `read` refused an unknown ID cleanly.
